title: Coronary Circulation & Myocardial Ischemia
subtitle: Week 03 · Lec 15 · Coronary Circulation & Myocardial Ischemia | 20 questions

questions.text: A cardiologist explains that coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) equals diastolic blood pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP). In which of the following clinical scenarios is CPP lowest?
options: Diastolic BP 60 mm Hg, LVEDP 25 mm Hg → CPP 35 mm Hg
Diastolic BP 70 mm Hg, LVEDP 12 mm Hg → CPP 58 mm Hg
Diastolic BP 80 mm Hg, LVEDP 10 mm Hg → CPP 70 mm Hg
Diastolic BP 65 mm Hg, LVEDP 5 mm Hg → CPP 60 mm Hg
questions.explanation:
Option A (CPP 35 mm Hg) is lowest because coronary perfusion pressure equals diastolic blood pressure minus LVEDP, and this scenario combines the lowest diastolic BP with the highest LVEDP among the choices. The formula (CPP = diastolic BP − LVEDP) is shown verbatim on Slide 34 with the example 80 − 10 = 70 mm Hg. The left ventricle perfuses predominantly during diastole, so diastolic pressure — not systolic — is the driving force. LVEDP acts as back-pressure opposing coronary inflow; a dilated or stiff left ventricle with elevated LVEDP (as in heart failure or diastolic dysfunction) therefore doubly impairs perfusion pressure by reducing the driving pressure (low diastolic BP) while raising the back-pressure (elevated LVEDP). CPP 35 mm Hg falls near the lower autoregulatory limit (~45 mm Hg, Slide 35) and would place this patient at high risk for subendocardial ischemia even at rest.
Option B is incorrect: CPP = 70 − 12 = 58 mm Hg, higher than Option A.
Option C is incorrect: CPP = 80 − 10 = 70 mm Hg, the illustrative example from Slide 34 and the highest CPP among the choices.
Option D is incorrect: CPP = 65 − 5 = 60 mm Hg, also higher than Option A.
Slide 34 · Transcript 31:42

questions.text: A 58-year-old man with stable coronary artery disease develops mid-substernal chest pressure whenever his heart rate reaches 135/min during exercise. His resting heart rate is 68/min. According to the determinants of myocardial oxygen demand, which mechanism most directly accounts for his angina threshold?
options: Augmented stroke volume from Starling's law as venous return rises during exercise
Proportional rise in myocardial oxygen consumption matching the near-doubling of heart rate
Sympathetic-mediated constriction of epicardial conduit arteries limiting coronary supply
Shortened diastole concentrating systolic compression of subendocardial microvessels beneath the ischemia threshold
questions.explanation:
Myocardial oxygen consumption (MVO2) rises in direct proportion to heart rate, so nearly doubling heart rate from 68 to 135 bpm nearly doubles total oxygen demand, precipitating angina when the fixed stenotic supply cannot match. Slide 28 lists three determinants of MVO2: heart rate, contractility, and wall tension, with heart rate listed first and described as increasing “directly in proportion” to MVO2. This is the primary mechanism behind exertional angina in fixed obstructive CAD: demand rises steeply with heart rate while the stenosis prevents a proportional increase in supply.
Option A is incorrect: stroke volume is not listed among MVO2 determinants on Slide 28; preload influences wall tension (via Laplace, Slide 31), which is a determinant, but augmented SV alone does not directly parallel heart rate in raising MVO2 per beat.
Option C is incorrect: Slide 23 states that large visible epicardial arteries are conduit vessels “not responsible for resistance to flow (when normal)”; sympathetic tone primarily affects arterioles, and epicardial constriction is not the taught mechanism here.
Option D is incorrect: shortened diastole does reduce subendocardial perfusion time (supply side, Slide 27), but the question asks which mechanism most directly explains the angina threshold, which is the demand side rise (Slide 28).
Slide 28 · Transcript 24:58

questions.text: A 55-year-old woman is found to have a 40% diameter stenosis of the left anterior descending artery on CT angiography. She has no symptoms at rest or with mild exertion. Which of the following best explains why she remains asymptomatic despite the anatomic stenosis?
options: The stenosis lies below 50%, so it cannot restrict coronary flow at any workload
Epicardial arteries normally account for most coronary vascular resistance, so 40% narrowing has no hemodynamic effect
Distal arterioles have dilated to compensate for the increased resistance imposed by the epicardial stenosis
Coronary autoregulation restores normal flow by raising systemic blood pressure to overcome the stenotic gradient
questions.explanation:
Distal arteriolar dilation compensates for the resistance imposed by the mild epicardial stenosis, preserving resting and low-exertion coronary flow. Slide 24 explains that once epicardial arteries become stenotic, resistance to flow increases “unless distal, small arterioles are able to dilate to compensate.” In the normal state, small arterioles — not epicardial conduits — are the principal resistance vessels (Slide 24). Atherosclerosis (an abnormal state) adds epicardial resistance, but arteriolar vasodilation can offset this up to a point; the patient is asymptomatic because her arterioles have sufficient vasodilatory reserve to maintain flow at this degree of stenosis. As the stenosis worsens or exertion increases demand, this reserve is exhausted and ischemia develops.
Option A is incorrect: while coronary flow reserve is preserved until approximately 70% stenosis (Slide 45), this does not mean that 40% stenosis imposes no resistance at any workload; rather, arteriolar compensation is masking the resistance, not its absence.
Option B is incorrect: Slide 24 explicitly states that small, distal arterioles — not epicardial arteries — make up the major resistance to flow in the normal state; epicardial conduits only acquire significant resistance when stenosed by atherosclerosis.
Option D is incorrect: coronary autoregulation adjusts arteriolar vasomotor tone to maintain constant flow independent of perfusion pressure (Slide 35); it operates by vasodilation, not by raising systemic blood pressure.
Slide 24 · Transcript 23:24

questions.text: During cardiac catheterization, phasic coronary blood flow tracings for a patient show that left ventricular coronary flow peaks in a specific phase of the cardiac cycle. In which phase does LV coronary perfusion predominantly occur, and why?
options: Systole; because aortic pressure peaks during systole and directly drives coronary flow into the left ventricular myocardium
Systole; because left ventricular wall relaxation during this phase opens subendocardial capillaries to inflow
Diastole only in hypertensive patients; in normotensive individuals systolic perfusion predominates due to the open aortic valve
Diastole; because systolic intramyocardial compression impedes LV coronary flow, especially in the subendocardium
questions.explanation:
The left ventricle is perfused predominantly during diastole because systolic intramyocardial compression — highest in the subendocardium, where wall stress is greatest — impedes coronary inflow during each systolic ejection phase. Slide 27 illustrates phasic flow through the coronary capillaries, and the professor explicitly corrected the misconception at Transcript 26:44: “It’s not when they profuse, it’s during diastole.” Although aortic pressure is highest during systole, the contracting LV generates intramyocardial wall stress that collapses intramural vessels, particularly in the inner wall where compressive forces are greatest. The subendocardium therefore has the least perfusion reserve and is the first region to become ischemic when diastolic time is shortened (e.g., tachycardia) or when LVEDP rises and reduces coronary perfusion pressure.
Option A is incorrect: while high aortic systolic pressure could theoretically drive coronary flow, systolic compression of the LV wall counteracts it, especially subendocardially; net LV coronary flow is lower during systole than diastole.
Option B is incorrect: LV wall relaxation occurs during diastole, not systole; systole is the contraction phase during which wall stress is highest and subendocardial vessels are compressed.
Option C is incorrect: the diastolic predominance of LV perfusion is a universal physiological property, not restricted to hypertensive patients; hypertension may worsen supply-demand balance but does not reverse the basic phasic perfusion pattern.
Slide 27 · Transcript 26:44

questions.text: Coronary autoregulation maintains constant myocardial blood flow matched to metabolic demand, independent of perfusion pressure. Over which approximate range of mean aortic pressures does this mechanism remain effective?
options: 45 to 150 mm Hg
60 to 120 mm Hg
30 to 100 mm Hg
70 to 200 mm Hg
questions.explanation:
Coronary autoregulation maintains perfusion at mean aortic pressures as low as 45 mm Hg and as high as 150 mm Hg, the range stated verbatim in Slide 35. The mechanism is intrinsic to the coronary vasculature: arterioles adjust their tone in response to local metabolites (adenosine, oxygen tension, lactate, H+, nitric oxide) so that flow matches demand regardless of upstream pressure within this range. Below 45 mm Hg, vasodilatory reserve is exhausted and flow falls with pressure; above 150 mm Hg, passive pressure distension overrides myogenic constriction and flow rises passively. Clinically, patients with critical coronary stenoses have exhausted arteriolar reserve downstream from the lesion, effectively operating below the autoregulatory plateau even at normal perfusion pressures.
Option B (60–120 mm Hg) is incorrect: this range is narrower than taught and resembles renal autoregulation ranges rather than the coronary-specific values on Slide 35.
Option C (30–100 mm Hg) is incorrect: the lower limit is too low; below approximately 45 mm Hg, coronary autoregulation fails and ischemia occurs.
Option D (70–200 mm Hg) is incorrect: the lower limit is too high and the upper limit exceeds the taught ceiling; autoregulation begins to fail well before 200 mm Hg.
Slide 35 · Transcript 31:19

questions.text: Coronary flow reserve (CFR) is the arteriolar vasodilatory capacity in response to increased myocardial oxygen demand. Which of the following correctly states both its definition and its characteristic ratio values?
options: Maximum flow divided by resting flow; approximately 1.5–2.0 experimentally, 1.0–1.5 when measured clinically
Resting flow divided by maximum flow; approximately 0.2–0.25 (the inverse of vasodilatory capacity)
Maximum flow divided by resting flow; approximately 4–5 experimentally, 2.25–2.5 when measured clinically
Maximum flow minus resting flow; expressed in absolute units (cc/min/100 g) rather than as a ratio
questions.explanation:
Coronary flow reserve is expressed as the ratio of maximum flow to resting (baseline) flow and is approximately 4–5 in experimental preparations and 2.25–2.5 when measured clinically, as stated on Slide 43. The difference between experimental and clinical values reflects methodological factors: experimental preparations can achieve complete pharmacologic vasodilation under controlled conditions, while clinical measurements (e.g., with adenosine or dipyridamole) are constrained by the patient’s hemodynamic state and residual vascular tone. A CFR below approximately 2.0 is generally considered impaired in clinical practice and correlates with inducible ischemia. The ratio is meaningful because it quantifies how much additional flow the arteriolar bed can recruit beyond its resting state before vasodilatory reserve is exhausted.
Option A is incorrect: the ratios 1.5–2.0 / 1.0–1.5 are substantially lower than the values on Slide 43; a CFR of 1.5 would indicate severely impaired reserve in a clinical patient.
Option B is incorrect: CFR is maximum/baseline, not the inverse; inverting the ratio would describe the fraction of maximum flow present at rest, not vasodilatory capacity.
Option D is incorrect: CFR is a dimensionless ratio (maximum/resting), not an absolute flow difference; expressing it in cc/min/100 g would be body-size dependent and not comparable across patients.
Slide 43 · Transcript 32:39

questions.text: A patient undergoes coronary catheterization and is found to have a 55% diameter stenosis in the right coronary artery. His resting fractional flow reserve is borderline. Which statement best describes the general relationship between coronary stenosis severity and blood flow indices?
options: CFR begins to fall at approximately 50% stenosis; resting flow is preserved until 70% stenosis
CFR is preserved until approximately 70% stenosis; resting flow is maintained until approximately 90% stenosis
Both CFR and resting flow decline together starting at approximately 60% stenosis
CFR is fully preserved until approximately 80% stenosis while resting flow is maintained until the artery is nearly completely occluded at 95%
questions.explanation:
Coronary flow reserve is preserved until approximately 70% diameter stenosis; resting coronary flow remains normal until approximately 90% stenosis — by which point maximum vasodilatory flow has already fallen steeply. This is the key clinical implication of the CFR curve shown on Slide 45 (“CFR preserved until 70% stenosis”), emphasized with an exam callout at Transcript 35:32. The stepwise pattern explains why: (1) patients with mild-to-moderate stenoses (50–70%) may have no resting symptoms but develop ischemia on stress testing as arteriolar reserve is exhausted; (2) patients with severe stenoses (>70%) have impaired CFR and may have resting symptoms; (3) only at near-total occlusion (>90%) does resting flow itself fall, causing rest angina or acute MI. This framework also explains why a 55% stenosis can produce a borderline functional test — the lesion is in the range where reserve may be reduced but resting flow intact.
Option A is incorrect: CFR begins to fall closer to 70%, not 50%; a 50% stenosis is generally hemodynamically less significant and is often managed medically without revascularization.
Option C is incorrect: resting flow and CFR do not decline together; resting flow is maintained by arteriolar vasodilation well beyond the stenosis threshold at which CFR first falls.
Option D is incorrect: the 80% and 95% thresholds are too permissive; the slide explicitly states CFR is preserved until 70% stenosis, not 80%.
Slide 45 · Transcript 35:32

questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with a 15-year history of hypertension and documented left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) develops chest tightness at lower exertion levels than expected. Her coronary angiogram shows no obstructive epicardial disease. Which of the following best explains her reduced exertional tolerance?
options: Hypertension causes epicardial coronary vasoconstriction through elevated circulating angiotensin II
LVH reduces capillary density in the myocardium, lowering oxygen extraction capacity at any given workload
Elevated systemic vascular resistance in hypertension directly occludes arteriolar flow, leaving no reserve for additional dilation during exercise
LVH increases resting MVO2 and reduces maximum coronary flow capacity, shrinking coronary flow reserve
questions.explanation:
Left ventricular hypertrophy reduces coronary flow reserve by simultaneously raising resting myocardial oxygen demand (through increased wall tension per the Laplace law) and limiting maximum coronary flow capacity, narrowing the reserve from both sides. Slide 46 illustrates that CFR can be squeezed by conditions that either raise resting flow or cap maximum flow. LVH is explicitly listed as a condition that lowers maximum achievable flow (increased extravascular compression from the thickened wall) while also raising resting MVO2 (the hypertrophied muscle consumes more oxygen at any given load via increased wall tension, Slides 28 and 31). The result is a reduced gap between resting and maximum flow — the patient’s reserve is exhausted at lower workloads, producing ischemia despite angiographically normal epicardial arteries.
Option A is incorrect: angiotensin II causes systemic vasoconstriction but not selective epicardial coronary constriction; the lecture does not identify this as a mechanism reducing CFR.
Option B is incorrect as stated: while capillary rarefaction in LVH is a real phenomenon, the lecture’s taught mechanism on Slide 46 is the combination of increased wall tension raising resting MVO2 and increased extravascular compression limiting maximum flow.
Option C is incorrect: elevated systemic vascular resistance does not directly occlude coronary arterioles; coronary autoregulation is independent of peripheral SVR within the 45–150 mm Hg MAP range (Slide 35), and this is not the taught mechanism for LVH-related CFR reduction.
Slide 46 · Transcript 39:29

questions.text: Coronary dominance is determined by a specific anatomical feature, and one artery type is dominant in the large majority of people. Which of the following correctly identifies both the defining feature and its prevalence?
options: The artery giving off the posterior interventricular (descending) branch; right coronary artery dominant in approximately 85% of cases
The artery supplying the greatest left ventricular myocardial mass; left anterior descending dominant in most individuals
The artery with the largest caliber at its coronary ostium; left main artery dominant in virtually all cases
The artery supplying both posterior papillary muscles and the basal inferior left ventricular wall simultaneously; codominant in most individuals
questions.explanation:
Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives off the posterior interventricular (descending) branch (PDA), which supplies the posterior basal ventricular septum; the right coronary artery is dominant in approximately 85% of people. Slide 20 states verbatim: “The term ‘dominant’ is used to refer to the coronary artery giving off the posterior interventricular (descending) branch, which supplies the posterior [basal] part of the ventricular septum and often part of the posterolateral wall of the left ventricle.” The prevalence breakdown from Slide 20: right dominant 85%, left circumflex dominant 8%, codominant 7%. The professor emphasized this explicitly at Transcript 18:45: “dominance is something you need to know.” Clinically, right dominance means an RCA occlusion can produce inferior MI plus posterior septal ischemia (PDA territory), while left dominant patients suffer larger LCx-territory infarcts with RCA occlusions affecting smaller regions.
Option B is incorrect: dominance is not defined by myocardial mass supplied; the LAD supplies the largest territory but “dominance” has a specific anatomical definition tied to the PDA origin, not to mass.
Option C is incorrect: caliber at the ostium is not how dominance is defined; the left main is present in all but has specific anatomy and is not described as “dominant.”
Option D is incorrect: supplying both posterior papillary muscles simultaneously would describe codominance or left dominance in specific cases, not the standard 85% right-dominant anatomy; the definition rests on PDA origin, not papillary muscle supply.
Slide 20 · Transcript 18:45

questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with an anterior STEMI. Echocardiography shows new wall motion abnormalities involving the anterior wall, anteroseptum, and apex of the left ventricle. Which coronary artery is most likely responsible?
options: Left circumflex artery
Right coronary artery
Left main artery with isolated circumflex territory sparing
Left anterior descending artery
questions.explanation:
The left anterior descending (LAD) artery supplies the anterior wall, anteroseptum, and apex of the left ventricle — the territory precisely described in this patient’s echocardiogram. Slide 17 maps coronary territories explicitly, and the professor emphasized this at Transcript 15:41: “Now, why is that important? Because where the anatomy helps diagnose the culprit artery.” The LAD courses down the anterior interventricular groove, giving off diagonal branches to the anterior LV wall and septal perforators to the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum; its distal segment wraps around the apex. Identifying the territory of dysfunction therefore identifies the culprit vessel without angiography, guiding emergent catheterization planning.
Option A is incorrect: the left circumflex (LCx) supplies the lateral LV wall and, in left-dominant individuals, the inferior wall; anteroseptal and apical territory is not its distribution.
Option B is incorrect: the right coronary artery supplies the inferior wall, posterior septum (via PDA in right-dominant individuals), and posterior papillary muscle; anterior and apical wall motion abnormalities are not the RCA territory.
Option C is incorrect: left main occlusion would produce a much larger territory involving both LAD and LCx distributions with anterior, lateral, and often inferior involvement; isolated anteroseptal/apical involvement points to the LAD, not the left main.
Slide 17 · Transcript 15:41

questions.text: A patient develops new lateral wall ST depressions and a lateral wall motion abnormality on stress echocardiography. Which coronary artery is most likely responsible for this ischemic territory?
options: Right coronary artery
Left circumflex artery
Left anterior descending artery at its most distal diagonal branch territory
Posterior descending artery in a right-dominant coronary circulation
questions.explanation:
The left circumflex (LCx) artery supplies the lateral left ventricular wall; new lateral ischemia points to LCx territory disease. Slide 17 maps the LCx to the lateral aspects of the LV, and the professor confirmed this at Transcript 16:09: “the circumflex supplies the lateral aspects here.” The LCx courses in the left atrioventricular groove and gives off obtuse marginal branches to the lateral and posterior LV wall. In a left-dominant individual, the LCx also gives off the PDA supplying the inferior wall and posterior septum; but even in standard right-dominant anatomy, the lateral wall is the LCx territory.
Option A is incorrect: the RCA supplies the inferior wall, right ventricle, and posterior septum (via PDA in right-dominant cases); lateral wall ischemia is not the RCA territory.
Option C is incorrect: the LAD diagonal branches supply the anterolateral wall, not the true lateral wall; new pure lateral ischemia (V5–V6 territory) is characteristic of LCx disease, not LAD diagonal territory.
Option D is incorrect: the posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and posterior interventricular septum, not the lateral LV wall; lateral ischemia in a right-dominant system is LCx territory.
Slide 17 · Transcript 16:09

questions.text: A 70-year-old man with severe three-vessel coronary artery disease develops acute myocardial ischemia. His blood pressure drops to 82/58 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains why his low cardiac output will worsen the ongoing ischemia?
options: Decreased heart rate through baroreceptor-mediated reflex bradycardia reduces myocardial oxygen demand
Elevated LVEDP from acute diastolic dysfunction compresses subendocardial vessels and directly impairs arterial inflow
Reduced cardiac output lowers coronary perfusion pressure, perpetuating the ischemic cycle
Increased systemic vascular resistance compensates for the low output by redistributing flow toward the coronary circulation
questions.explanation:
Systolic dysfunction from ischemia decreases cardiac output, which in turn decreases coronary perfusion pressure, further impairing myocardial blood supply and worsening ischemia — the systolic arm of the self-perpetuating cascade described on Slide 52. Slide 52 states explicitly: “systolic dysfunction (loss of contraction) → decrease cardiac output → decrease coronary perfusion pressure.” Since CPP = diastolic BP − LVEDP (Slide 34), a fall in cardiac output causing hypotension directly reduces the numerator of the perfusion pressure equation, starving the ischemic myocardium of flow at the moment it is most vulnerable. This is the systolic arm of the “ischemia begets ischemia” cycle (Slide 51–52).
Option A is incorrect: baroreceptor-mediated bradycardia in hypotensive acute ischemia is not the dominant response; sympathetic activation dominates, raising heart rate and MVO2 further (the catecholamine arm of Slide 52).
Option B is incorrect: elevated LVEDP from diastolic dysfunction does worsen CPP, but this is the diastolic arm of the cascade; the question specifically asks about the consequence of reduced cardiac output (systolic arm). The two arms reinforce each other but are distinct mechanisms on Slide 52.
Option D is incorrect: redistributed peripheral vasoconstriction (high SVR) accompanies cardiogenic shock but does not preferentially redirect flow to the coronary arteries; coronary perfusion pressure falls with systemic hypotension regardless of SVR.
Slide 52

questions.text: During an episode of acute myocardial ischemia, a 68-year-old woman develops sudden-onset dyspnea. Her oxygen saturation drops from 98% to 91% and her chest radiograph shows pulmonary vascular congestion. Which mechanism best explains this sequence?
options: Impaired LV relaxation from ischemia raises LVEDP and pulmonary capillary pressure, causing congestion and reduced arterial oxygen delivery
Ischemia-induced mitral valve prolapse through papillary muscle rupture produces acute severe regurgitation and flash pulmonary edema
Ischemia triggers reflex bronchospasm via vagal pathways, reducing alveolar ventilation and oxygenation
Systolic dysfunction reduces right ventricular output, causing retrograde pulmonary arterial pressure elevation and alveolar congestion from the right side
questions.explanation:
Ischemia impairs LV relaxation (diastolic dysfunction), raising LVEDP and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure for any given volume, which drives fluid into the alveoli and reduces arterial oxygen delivery — the diastolic arm of the ischemic cascade on Slide 52. Slide 52 describes the sequence: diastolic dysfunction (loss of relaxation) → higher LVEDP/PCWP for any given volume → dyspnea, decreased pO2, decreased O2 delivery → increased wall tension (increased MVO2). This is a critical feedforward loop: diastolic dysfunction raises wall tension (Laplace law, Slide 31), which raises MVO2, which worsens ischemia, which worsens diastolic dysfunction. The resulting pulmonary congestion also reduces arterial oxygen saturation, further limiting myocardial oxygen supply.
Option B is incorrect: acute papillary muscle rupture causing severe MR is a mechanical complication of MI, not the initial mechanism of ischemia-induced dyspnea in the first minutes of an ischemic episode; furthermore, rupture implies transmural necrosis, not early ischemia.
Option C is incorrect: reflex bronchospasm is not a taught mechanism on Slide 52; the pulmonary congestion in ischemia-induced dyspnea is hemodynamic (elevated LVEDP), not bronchospastic.
Option D is incorrect: the immediate consequence of LV ischemia is left-sided diastolic dysfunction raising pulmonary CAPILLARY pressure (left-heart back-pressure), not primary right ventricular failure causing pulmonary arterial hypertension from the right side.
Slide 52

questions.text: A pathologist reviews coronary angiograms from patients who suffered myocardial infarction and classifies the culprit lesions by pre-infarct stenosis severity. Which of the following best describes the distribution of stenosis severity at the culprit site prior to MI, based on the Falk et al. data presented in the lecture?
options: Approximately 50% of MIs occur at stenoses greater than 70%, reflecting the importance of critical obstructive disease
Approximately 68% of MIs arise at stenoses less than 50% diameter, with only 18% at stenoses greater than 70%
Roughly equal proportions of MIs occur at stenoses below 50%, between 50–70%, and above 70% diameter
Nearly all MIs occur at stenoses exceeding 90% diameter because only near-total occlusion produces resting ischemia sufficient to trigger infarction
questions.explanation:
Approximately 68% of myocardial infarctions arise from coronary stenoses of less than 50% diameter, demonstrating that it is vulnerable soft-plaque rupture — not critical flow-limiting stenosis — that causes most heart attacks. Slide 54 (Falk et al., Circulation 1995) presents the breakdown: 68% at <50% stenosis, 14% at 50–70%, and 18% at >70%. This counterintuitive finding is clinically fundamental: patients with non-obstructive plaques on stress tests or angiography remain at high risk from the 68% majority of infarcts that arise from soft, lipid-rich plaques with thin fibrous caps that rupture without prior hemodynamic significance. The professor underscored this at Transcript 43:41: “plaque, what causes your heart attack?” — the answer is plaque rupture, not the stenosis degree.
Option A is incorrect: only 18% of MIs occur at >70% stenosis; framing >70% stenoses as responsible for “approximately 50%” of MIs overstates the critical-stenosis contribution by nearly threefold.
Option C is incorrect: the distribution is far from equal; the <50% group accounts for 68%, a dominant majority, not one-third.
Option D is incorrect: near-total occlusion (>90%) is when resting flow falls (Slide 45), but the MI data (Slide 54) show that most infarcts happen from plaques far below this threshold; the plaque rupture mechanism operates independently of resting stenosis severity.
Slide 54 · Transcript 43:41

questions.text: A 47-year-old man reports chest discomfort that occurs with exertion and resolves completely with rest. He has never tried nitroglycerin. He describes the quality as sharp and stabbing rather than pressure or squeezing. Using the clinical classification of chest pain from the lecture, how would this presentation be categorized?
options: Noncardiac chest pain, because exertional onset alone is not sufficient for any angina classification
Typical angina, because exertional onset qualifies even if the other criteria are not met
Typical angina requiring no further workup because all three criteria are implied by exertional symptoms
Atypical angina, because 2 of the 3 criteria for typical angina are met.
questions.explanation:
Atypical angina: this presentation meets 2 of the 3 typical angina criteria (exertional provocation and rest relief) but fails criterion 1 because sharp, stabbing quality is not a characteristic anginal descriptor. Slide 56 defines the three-tier classification by three criteria: (1) substernal chest discomfort with a characteristic quality and duration, (2) provoked by exertion or emotional stress, and (3) relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. This patient satisfies criterion 2 (exertional onset) and criterion 3 (resolves with rest). However, criterion 1 requires a characteristic quality — Slide 57 identifies the canonical anginal quality as “squeezing, pressure-like in quality (closed fist = Levine’s sign)”; sharp and stabbing are atypical descriptors that do not meet this criterion. Two of three criteria met = atypical angina by Slide 56 definition.
CategoryCriteria met
Typical anginaAll 3
Atypical angina2 of 3
Noncardiac chest pain1 or none

Option A is incorrect: this patient meets criteria 2 and 3, placing him in the atypical angina category; noncardiac chest pain requires only 1 or none of the three criteria, which is not the case here.
Option B is incorrect: typical angina requires ALL three criteria; criterion 1 is unmet because sharp, stabbing quality does not satisfy “characteristic quality and duration” on Slide 56, as confirmed by the squeezing/pressure-like description on Slide 57.
Option C is incorrect: typical angina cannot be inferred from exertional symptoms alone; all three criteria must be explicitly satisfied, and criterion 1 fails here.
Slide 56 · Slide 57

questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents to clinic with episodic chest discomfort. He places his closed fist against his sternum while describing the sensation. The episodes last approximately 8 minutes, are provoked by climbing stairs, and resolve with rest. He denies radiation. Which of the following additional features, if present, would best support a classic stable angina diagnosis based on the lecture’s symptom criteria?
options: Sharp, pleuritic quality worsened by deep inspiration and lying flat
Reproducible nocturnal awakening at the same time each night unrelated to exertion
Radiation to the left arm or jaw with associated diaphoresis, provoked by cold weather or large meals
Onset at rest with duration exceeding 20 minutes and failure to abate with three sublingual nitroglycerin tablets
questions.explanation:
Radiation to the left arm or jaw with diaphoresis, provoked by cold weather or large meals, represents additional features of classic stable angina as listed on Slide 57. The patient’s fist against his sternum is Levine’s sign — a hallmark of anginal quality described on Slide 57 as “squeezing, pressure-like in quality (closed fist = Levine’s sign).” Slide 57 enumerates classic stable angina features: mid-substernal pressure, 2–20 minute duration, radiation to left arm/neck/jaw/back, associated shortness of breath/sweating/nausea, exacerbated by exertion/cold/meals/stress, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. The professor identified these as “the classic anginal symptoms” at Transcript 49:53. Option C adds radiation and diaphoresis plus two classic triggers (cold, meals) that align directly with the Slide 57 symptom list.
Option A is incorrect: sharp, pleuritic quality worsened by inspiration and lying flat is characteristic of pericarditis or pleuritis, not angina; angina is pressure-like, not pleuritic.
Option B is incorrect: reproducible nocturnal episodes unrelated to exertion suggest Prinzmetal’s variant angina (coronary vasospasm) or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, not classic stable exertional angina; stable angina is specifically effort-related.
Option D is incorrect: onset at rest lasting >20 minutes and failing 3 sublingual NTG tablets are defining features of unstable angina or NSTEMI (Slide 60), not stable angina; these features would trigger urgent ACS evaluation and reclassify the presentation.
Slide 57 · Transcript 49:53

questions.text: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 3-week history of jaw pain, fatigue, and nausea that occurs with exertion. She denies chest pain or pressure. A resting ECG shows no acute changes. Which of the following best explains her presentation?
options: Women, elderly patients, and diabetics commonly present with atypical angina symptoms such as jaw pain, nausea, and fatigue rather than classic substernal chest pressure
Her symptoms suggest a non-cardiac cause because exertional jaw pain without chest pain cannot represent myocardial ischemia
Diabetic neuropathy prevents perception of exertional symptoms, so her presentation cannot be anginal in origin
Jaw pain and nausea are specifically characteristic of right ventricular ischemia, not the typical left ventricular territory ischemia seen in CAD
questions.explanation:
Women, elderly patients, and diabetics classically present with atypical angina symptoms — including jaw pain, fatigue, nausea, and dyspnea — instead of the classic mid-substernal pressure described in the standard angina semiology. The professor emphasized this three times between Transcript 47:53 and 48:49, calling it a “classic different presentation” for women. Slide 57 lists these atypical manifestations. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy blunts pain perception, making painless or atypical ischemia common; women have higher rates of microvascular and vasospastic disease with atypical symptoms; elderly patients may have reduced pain sensitivity. The clinical importance is that these patients are at higher risk of delayed diagnosis because their symptoms are dismissed as non-cardiac — the exact opposite of the correct approach.
Option B is incorrect: exertional jaw pain in a diabetic woman is a recognized anginal equivalent; the absence of typical substernal chest pain does not exclude cardiac ischemia, especially in the groups the professor highlighted as classically atypical.
Option C is incorrect: diabetic neuropathy reduces pain perception but does not eliminate symptoms entirely; atypical symptoms (fatigue, jaw pain, nausea) still occur and are specifically taught as anginal equivalents in diabetics; the statement overgeneralizes.
Option D is incorrect: jaw pain and nausea are not specific to right ventricular ischemia; they are classic radiation and associated symptom patterns in left ventricular ischemia, as listed on Slide 57 under stable angina symptoms.
Slide 57 · Transcript 47:53

questions.text: A 59-year-old man with known stable angina reports that over the past week he has been getting his typical chest pressure with walking only half a block, compared to two blocks previously. Last night the pressure awakened him from sleep and lasted 18 minutes. He took two sublingual nitroglycerin tablets with incomplete relief. How should this presentation be classified?
options: Stable angina with a new, lower exertion threshold requiring medication adjustment
Atypical angina because the nocturnal onset and rest symptoms suggest a non-obstructive etiology
Stable angina exacerbation requiring reassurance that the pain pattern remains benign
Unstable angina, because the presentation includes crescendo pattern, nocturnal rest onset, prolonged episode, and failure to abate with more than 2 sublingual nitroglycerin tablets
questions.explanation:
This presentation meets multiple criteria for unstable angina (UA) / NSTEMI as listed on Slide 60: decrease in exertion threshold (half block from two blocks), onset at rest (nocturnal awakening), prolonged episode (>10–15 minutes), and failure to abate with >2 sublingual nitroglycerin tablets. Slide 60 defines UA/NSTEMI symptoms as any of: new-onset angina, increase in frequency/duration/severity of prior angina, decrease in exertion required to provoke, any prolonged episode (>10–15 min), failure to abate with >2–3 S.L. NTG, or onset at rest or awakening from sleep. This patient fulfills at least four of these criteria simultaneously, making this unambiguously unstable angina requiring urgent evaluation. The key discriminator from stable angina is the pattern change: stable angina is reproducible and predictable; UA represents a new, unstable pattern from plaque instability.
Option A is incorrect: a decreased exertion threshold over one week, combined with a nocturnal rest episode lasting 18 minutes and partial NTG response, is not a stable angina medication-adjustment scenario; these are ACS warning signs that require urgent evaluation, not outpatient adjustment.
Option B is incorrect: nocturnal rest symptoms and prolonged duration are listed on Slide 60 as UA/NSTEMI criteria; classifying this as atypical angina would miss the ACS diagnosis.
Option C is incorrect: the new crescendo pattern and nocturnal rest episode represent plaque destabilization, which is explicitly the distinguishing feature of unstable from stable angina; reassurance is contraindicated here.

questions.text: A 66-year-old man suffers a large acute MI. An echocardiogram performed 4 hours later estimates that approximately 25% of the left ventricular myocardium is non-contractile. Which of the following outcomes is most consistent with this finding?
options: Homeostasis is achieved with no hemodynamic consequence because 25% LV involvement falls below the threshold for clinical sequelae
Cardiogenic shock, because any MI affecting more than 20% of the LV leads to hemodynamic collapse
Congestive heart failure, because infarction of more than 20% of the LV leads to heart failure while collapse requires more than 40%
Sudden death from arrhythmia, because the wavefront of necrosis reaching 25% of the LV wall creates sufficient heterogeneity to trigger ventricular fibrillation
questions.explanation:
Infarction of more than 20% of the left ventricle leads to congestive heart failure; hemodynamic collapse requires more than 40% LV involvement — and this patient’s 25% estimate crosses the CHF threshold but not the collapse threshold. Slide 64 states: “If large area of infarction (>20% LV) → Congestive heart failure; If larger area of infarction (>40% LV) → hemodynamic collapse.” The ischemic wavefront propagates from the subendocardium outward to the epicardium (the wavefront phenomenon, Slide 64), and the cumulative LV mass involved determines the hemodynamic consequence. At 25% involvement, the damaged left ventricle can no longer maintain adequate forward cardiac output, producing elevated LVEDP and PCWP (pulmonary back-pressure) and reduced organ perfusion (CHF), but the remaining 75% of functioning LV myocardium is sufficient to prevent the complete circulatory collapse that accompanies >40% involvement.
Option A is incorrect: 25% LV involvement exceeds the 20% threshold for CHF on Slide 64; this amount of infarction is not hemodynamically silent.
Option B is incorrect: cardiogenic shock / hemodynamic collapse requires infarction of >40% of the LV per Slide 64; 25% is above the CHF threshold but below the collapse threshold.
Option D is incorrect: while large MI does increase arrhythmia risk, the lecture’s specific taught thresholds on Slide 64 are the 20% (CHF) and 40% (hemodynamic collapse) LV area criteria, not a 25% arrhythmia threshold; the wavefront phenomenon describes the spatial progression of necrosis, not an arrhythmia trigger per se.

questions.text: During open-heart surgery, the perfusionist needs to deliver cardioplegic solution retrogradely through the main cardiac venous drainage structure. Which vessel receives this catheter, and into which cardiac chamber does it empty?
options: Great cardiac vein, emptying into the left atrium
Coronary sinus, emptying into the right atrium
Thebesian veins, emptying diffusely through the myocardium into all cardiac chambers
Anterior cardiac veins, emptying directly into the right ventricle and bypassing the coronary sinus
questions.explanation:
The coronary sinus is the principal venous drainage structure of the heart, receiving blood from the great, middle, and small cardiac veins, and empties into the right atrium — making it the correct target for retrograde cardioplegia. The professor identified the coronary sinus as “the most important” cardiac venous structure at Transcript 18:35. In retrograde cardioplegia, a catheter placed in the coronary sinus delivers cardioplegic solution upstream through the venous system into the capillaries, providing myocardial protection during cardiopulmonary bypass. Because the solution flows retrogradely through capillaries into arterioles, it reaches ischemic territories even if epicardial arteries are severely stenosed — an advantage over antegrade aortic root delivery.
Option A is incorrect: the great cardiac vein is one tributary of the coronary sinus, not the main structure; the coronary sinus is the principal collecting vessel that then empties into the right atrium, not the left.
Option C is incorrect: Thebesian veins are small venous channels that drain directly into the cardiac chambers, but they are minor contributions to venous drainage and are not the principal structure used for retrograde cardioplegia.
Option D is incorrect: while some anterior cardiac veins do drain directly into the right ventricle, this is a minor pathway; the coronary sinus is the dominant venous drainage route and the clinical target for retrograde cardioplegia.
